title: Recipes by kind of op
intro: Each recipe is a plan for a kind of op, with a skeleton that passed the unedited simulator check on a worked op. Change the shapes and the arithmetic for your op and keep the structure.

Each heading says what was checked. `[passes the simulator]`: the unedited check passed on every input set. The second tag names the chip package of this run and says whether its compiler accepted the skeleton. That compile was made with no chip. It shows the compiler accepts every call in the skeleton and wrote kernel source. It does not show that the kernel runs on a chip or gives the right numbers there.

A line that starts with `The chip compiler refuses` is a form that was tried against that compiler and failed. Where an entry of the sheet above says something else about the chip, follow these lines: they were compiled.

recipes.name: row-reduce-spread
recipes.title: Reduce each row to one value, then use it across the row
recipes.applies_to: an op where every output value depends on a total over its row (a norm, a mean, a normalisation)
recipes.worked_op: L2-normalise each row: out = x * rsqrt(sum of x squared over the row + 1e-6)
plan: One buffer block is a whole row of tiles, shape (1, col_tiles). The data is read once, and the same block feeds the reduction and the finishing expression: a block can be used in several statements while its `with` stays open.
Reduce over the last dimension with shape (1, 1). The result is one value per row, in column 0 of a one-tile block.

A Python number is not an operand. Make a (1, 1) block with `ttl.block.fill(value, shape=(1, 1))` for a constant such as an epsilon or 1/N. Take N from `x.shape[1]`, which counts elements, before you divide.
Multiply the reduction's result by a (1, 1) block before you add to it or pass it to a function: 1/N for a mean, 1.0 when there is nothing to scale. Then add the epsilon and take the function.
Spread the per-row value back with `ttl.block.broadcast(v, dims=[-1], shape=(1, col_tiles))`. It copies column 0 across the values of the row and across its tiles.
Finish with one elementwise expression and one `store` into the output block.
recipes.units: Buffer shapes and slices count tiles. `x.shape` counts elements.
skeleton: # One block is a whole row of tiles, so the sum and the scaling use the same block.
with x_dfb.wait() as x_blk, out_dfb.reserve() as out_blk:
# The row sum of squares: one value per row, in column 0 of a (1, 1) block.
# Multiply a reduction by a (1, 1) block before any other use (see the plan).
# Spread column 0 across the row's values and across its tiles.

recipes.name: column-reduce-accumulate
recipes.title: Reduce down the rows, over more tile rows than one block holds
recipes.applies_to: an op that totals each column (a column mean, a column sum, a variance down the rows)
recipes.worked_op: the mean of each column of a (128, 256) input, written to row 0 of a (32, 256) output
plan: Read the rows in blocks of R tile rows, shape (R, col_tiles). Reduce each block over dims=[0] with shape (1, col_tiles).

Keep a running total in a Python variable that starts as `ttl.block.fill(0.0, shape=(1, col_tiles))` and add each block's partial sum: `total += partial`. A block expression kept in a Python variable carries its value from one loop pass to the next.
Store once, after the loop, into the output block. Scale by 1/rows with a block of the same shape from `ttl.block.fill`.
After a reduction over dims=[0] the column totals are in row 0 of each result tile. In the simulator rows 1 to 31 of the tile are 0.
recipes.units: The count to divide by is `x.shape[0]`, in elements. Block and slice shapes count tiles.
skeleton: # Python arithmetic on element counts runs when the kernel is built.
# First pass: a running total of the partial column sums. A block expression kept in a
# Python variable carries its value from one loop pass to the next.
# Second step: scale the total by 1 / rows, with a block of the same shape.

negatives.name: no scaling
negatives.claim: A kernel that stores the total without dividing by the row count fails the check.

spec.description: out[0, j] = the mean of column j of x over its 128 rows; the other 31 rows of out are 0

compile_negatives.name: a division inside a thread
compile_negatives.claim: a division written inside a thread, as in `ttl.block.fill(1.0 / 128.0, ...)`: compute the number in the operation body, before the threads, as `inv_n` is.

recipes.name: elementwise-with-operands
recipes.title: An elementwise chain with a constant and a row of values reused for every row block
recipes.applies_to: an op built from several inputs, a constant, and a small operand that is repeated down the rows
recipes.worked_op: out = x * y * 0.5 + r, where the (32, 256) tensor r is repeated down the rows of x
plan: A constant is a block: `ttl.block.fill(0.5, shape=(1, col_tiles))`, the same shape as the other operands.

An operand that is one row of tiles and is used for every row block is read again for each block: `ttl.copy(r[0:1, 0:col_tiles], r_blk)` inside the row loop. All its 32 rows differ, so use it as it is.
Do not broadcast such an operand down the rows. `ttl.block.broadcast` also spreads values inside each tile, and that destroys a tile whose rows differ.
The three threads loop the same number of times, and every `reserve` has a matching `wait`.
recipes.units: Slices and buffer shapes count tiles.
skeleton: with x_dfb.reserve() as x_blk, y_dfb.reserve() as y_blk, r_dfb.reserve() as r_blk:
# r is one row of tiles whose 32 rows all differ and are used for every row block:
# read the same slice again each pass. A broadcast would also spread values
# inside each tile, which is wrong for an operand that varies by row.
# A Python number cannot be an operand: a constant is a block of the same shape.

recipes.name: running-total-down-rows
recipes.title: A value carried from one row block to the next
recipes.applies_to: an op where each row block depends on the blocks before it (a running total, a running update)
recipes.worked_op: out tile row t = the sum of x tile rows 0 to t, elementwise
plan: Start the carried value as `ttl.block.fill(0.0, shape=(1, col_tiles))` in a Python variable, before the loop and inside the compute thread.
In each pass: `total += x_blk`, then `out_blk.store(total)`. The variable keeps its value to the next pass.
The reader, the compute function and the writer loop the same number of times, once per row block.
recipes.units: The loop runs over tile rows, `x.shape[0] // TILE_SIZE` times.
